::: {.solutions}

Back in Session 1 we said *"$x$ is even"* is **not** a statement — it has no truth value until you say
what $x$ is. This session is about the words that fix that: **for all** and **there exists**. Put one in
front of an open sentence and it becomes a genuine statement, true or false.

They matter for two reasons. First, almost every theorem on Paper 2 secretly begins with one of them
(*"for all integers $n$…"*). Second — and this is where the marks are — **negating them is the engine
behind disproof.** To show a "for all" claim is false you produce **one** counterexample; that single
example *is* the negation. Get the negation rule wrong and you will hunt for the wrong thing.

::: {.callout-important}
## The two rules this session rests on

$$\textbf{not}\,\big(\textbf{for all } x,\; P\big) \;=\; \textbf{there exists } x \textbf{ such that } \textbf{not } P$$
$$\textbf{not}\,\big(\textbf{there exists } x,\; P\big) \;=\; \textbf{for all } x,\; \textbf{not } P$$

**Negating flips the quantifier *and* negates the inside.** "for all" becomes "there exists", "there
exists" becomes "for all" — and whatever was inside gets negated too.
:::

Specification: **Arg3** — *for all, for some (meaning for at least one), there exists*; &nbsp; **Arg4** —
*negate statements that use any of these*. Official source: **Notes on Logic and Proof**, pp. 56–63.

---

# Part 1 — Easy

## Question 1

::: {.question}
State whether each is **true** or **false**. In each case $x$ is real unless stated otherwise.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) For all real $x$, &nbsp; $x^2 \ge 0$. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) There exists a real $x$ such that $x^2 = 2$. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) For all integers $n$, &nbsp; $n^2 > n$. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(d) There exists an integer $n$ such that $n^2 = n$. **[1]**
:::

Two different jobs hide here, and knowing which you are doing halves the work. [To confirm a "for all"
statement you must argue it holds in **every** case; to knock it down you need just **one**
counterexample.]{.hl} A "there exists" statement is the mirror image — **one** example confirms it, but
knocking it down needs an argument covering everything.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — deciding whether a quantified statement is true
:::


**(a) True.** A square is never negative — this holds for every real $x$. *(A "for all" that really is
true, so no counterexample exists.)*

**(b) True.** $x = \sqrt2$ works: one example is all a "there exists" needs.

**(c) False.** It fails at $n = 1$: $1^2 = 1$, which is **not** $> 1$. *(It also fails at $n=0$.)* One
counterexample is enough to destroy a "for all".

**(d) True.** $n = 0$ works ($0^2 = 0$), and so does $n=1$. Either one confirms the "there exists".

$\blacksquare$

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| (c) called true because "$n^2>n$ usually" | *Usually* is not *for all*. A single failure ($n=1$) makes the whole statement false. |
| (b) needing to "solve for all $x$" | A "there exists" is satisfied by **one** witness. Produce it and stop. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — the two quantifiers, and what it takes to settle them

A quantifier turns an **open sentence** (one with a free $x$, no truth value) into a **statement**.

| Quantifier | Also written | Means |
|---|---|---|
| **for all $x$**, $P(x)$ | for every, for each | $P$ holds in *every* case |
| **there exists $x$**, $P(x)$ | for some, for at least one | $P$ holds in *at least one* case |

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**"for some" means "for at least one"** — the spec says so explicitly. It does **not** mean "for some but
not all". Even if $P$ happens to hold for *every* $x$, "there exists an $x$" is still true.
:::

**What it takes to prove or disprove each** — this table is the whole of proof and disproof on Paper 2:

| Statement | To **prove** it | To **disprove** it |
|---|---|---|
| for all $x$, $P(x)$ | a general argument covering **every** $x$ | **one counterexample** (an $x$ with $P$ false) |
| there exists $x$, $P(x)$ | **one witness** (an $x$ with $P$ true) | a general argument that $P$ fails for **every** $x$ |

Notice the diagonal symmetry: *proving* a "there exists" and *disproving* a "for all" are the same easy
job — find one example. That is why negation, which swaps the two, is so central.
:::

---

## Question 2

::: {.question}
Write the **negation** of each statement, as a positive sentence (no "it is not the case that").

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) For all real $x$, &nbsp; $x^2 > 0$. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) There exists an integer $n$ such that $n^2 = 5$. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) Every student passed the test. **[1]**
:::

Apply the two rules mechanically: [flip the quantifier, and negate what's inside]{.hl}. "For all" becomes
"there exists", "there exists" becomes "for all". The commonest error is negating only one of the two —
either flipping the quantifier but forgetting the inside, or vice versa. Do both, every time.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — negating a single quantifier
:::


**(a)** Flip *for all* → *there exists*, and negate $x^2>0$ to $x^2 \le 0$:

> **There exists a real $x$ such that $x^2 \le 0$.**

*(True, in fact — $x=0$.)* Note the negation of $>$ is $\le$, not $<$.

**(b)** Flip *there exists* → *for all*, and negate $n^2=5$ to $n^2 \ne 5$:

> **For all integers $n$, &nbsp; $n^2 \ne 5$.**

**(c)** "Every student passed" is a *for all*; its negation is a *there exists*:

> **There exists a student who did not pass** &nbsp;(i.e. **at least one** student failed).

$\blacksquare$

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| (a) negated to "there exists $x$ with $x^2 > 0$" | The quantifier was flipped but the **inside was not negated**. Both must change. |
| (a) inside negated to $x^2 < 0$ | The negation of $>$ is $\le$ — the boundary $x^2=0$ is included. |
| (c) "no student passed" | That is far too strong. The negation of "all passed" is "**at least one** failed", not "all failed". |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — the mechanical negation rule

$$\text{not}\big(\text{for all } x,\ P\big) = \text{there exists } x,\ \text{not } P$$
$$\text{not}\big(\text{there exists } x,\ P\big) = \text{for all } x,\ \text{not } P$$

**Two things change, always:**

1. the **quantifier flips** — ∀ ↔ ∃, "for all" ↔ "there exists";
2. the **inside is negated** — $P$ becomes not $P$.

Changing only one is the classic half-done negation, and it is wrong.

**Why it makes sense.** *"Not everything is $P$"* means *"something fails to be $P$"* — flip to "there
exists", negate inside. *"Nothing is $P$"* means *"everything fails to be $P$"* — flip to "for all",
negate inside. Say the sentence in plain English and the rule falls out.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Negating the inside correctly** matters as much as flipping the quantifier — the comparison-negations
from Session 2 return here:

| Inside | Its negation |
|---|---|
| $x > 0$ | $x \le 0$ |
| $x = 5$ | $x \ne 5$ |
| $x$ is even | $x$ is odd |
| $P$ **and** $Q$ | not $P$ **or** not $Q$ |
:::
:::

## Question 3

::: {.question}
Consider the statement: &nbsp; **All prime numbers are odd.**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Is it true or false? Justify your answer. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) Write its correct negation. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) A student says the negation is *"No prime number is odd."* Explain why that is wrong. **[1]**
:::

This is the single most common quantifier mistake, and the question is built around it. "All X are Y" is
a *for all* statement, so [its negation is a *there exists*, not another *for all*]{.hl}. "No X is Y" is
itself a "for all" (it says *every* X fails to be Y) — far too strong to be the negation. The true
negation asks only for **one** exception.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — why "not all X are Y" is not "no X is Y"
:::


**(a) False.** The prime $2$ is even, so not every prime is odd. That single prime settles it.

**(b)** "All primes are odd" is *for all primes $p$, $p$ is odd*. Negating:

> **There exists a prime that is not odd** &nbsp;(i.e. **at least one** prime is even — namely $2$).

**(c)** *"No prime is odd"* claims **every** prime is even — a "for all" statement, and a wildly false one
($3, 5, 7,\dots$ are all odd primes). The real negation of "all are odd" needs only **one** non-odd
prime, not *all* primes to be non-odd. [Negating a "for all" gives a "there exists", never another "for
all".]{.hl}

$\blacksquare$

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**The three-way distinction to hold onto.** For a property Y over a collection X:

- **"All X are Y"** — every one is Y.
- **"No X is Y"** — every one *fails* Y &nbsp;(the *opposite extreme*, also a "for all").
- **"Not all X are Y"** — *at least one* fails Y &nbsp;(the **negation** of the first, a "there exists").

"No X is Y" and "Not all X are Y" are completely different: the first is a strong claim about everything,
the second a weak claim about one thing.
:::

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| Negation of "all are odd" = "none are odd" | That is the opposite extreme, still a "for all". The negation is "**at least one** is not odd". |
| (a) trying to check every prime | One counterexample ($2$) is a complete disproof. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — "all", "none", "not all", "some not"

Picture the collection of X's. Each statement carves it differently:

| Statement | Picture | Quantifier type |
|---|---|---|
| **All** X are Y | every X is inside Y | for all |
| **No** X is Y | every X is outside Y | for all (of the negation) |
| **Some** X is Y | at least one X inside Y | there exists |
| **Not all** X are Y &nbsp;=&nbsp; **some** X is **not** Y | at least one X outside Y | there exists |

The two on the diagonal are negations of each other:

$$\text{not}(\text{all X are Y}) = \text{some X is not Y}, \qquad \text{not}(\text{some X is Y}) = \text{no X is Y}.$$

**"No X is Y" is the negation of "some X *is* Y"** — not of "all X are Y". Lining them up this way stops
the classic confusion for good.
:::

# Part 2 — Medium

## Question 4

::: {.question}
For each statement, decide whether it is true. If false, **disprove it with a counterexample**; if true,
give a one-line reason.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) For all real $x$, &nbsp; $x^2 > x$. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) For all real $x$, &nbsp; if $x > 1$ then $x^2 > x$. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) For all integers $n$, &nbsp; $n^2 + n$ is even. **[2]**
:::

Each is a "for all", so [disproving one means producing a single $x$ where it fails]{.hl} — and the place
to look is always the awkward region: small numbers, negatives, fractions, zero. Part (b) has a condition
attached ($x>1$), which shrinks where you are allowed to hunt: your counterexample must **satisfy $x>1$**
and still break the conclusion, or there is none.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — disproving a "for all" by counterexample
:::


**(a) False.** Counterexample $x = \tfrac12$: then $x^2 = \tfrac14$, which is **not** $> \tfrac12$.
*(Any $x$ with $0 < x < 1$ works; so does any negative $x$.)*

**(b) True.** If $x > 1$ then multiplying both sides of $x>1$ by the positive number $x$ gives $x^2 > x$.
*The condition $x>1$ rules out exactly the counterexamples that broke part (a).*

**(c) True.** $n^2 + n = n(n+1)$ is a product of two **consecutive** integers, one of which is always
even — so the product is even, for every $n$. *(No counterexample exists.)*

$\blacksquare$

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| (a) "disproved" with $x=2$ | $x=2$ gives $4>2$, which **satisfies** the statement. A counterexample must make it **fail**. |
| (b) counterexample $x = \tfrac12$ | Not allowed — it fails the condition $x>1$. Your example must satisfy the hypothesis. |
| (c) checking a few $n$ and asserting "true" | A few cases never prove a "for all". The $n(n+1)$ argument covers all $n$ at once. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:8cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — how to hunt a counterexample

To disprove **for all $x$, $P(x)$**, you need one $x$ with $P(x)$ **false**. Where to look, in order:

1. **Boundary and small values:** $0$, $1$, $-1$, $\tfrac12$.
2. **Negatives** — especially when the statement involves squares or square roots.
3. **The extremes** of any allowed range.

If the statement is **for all $x$, if $H(x)$ then $C(x)$** (a "for all" over an implication), your
counterexample must do **both**: satisfy the hypothesis $H$ **and** break the conclusion $C$. An $x$ that
fails $H$ proves nothing — the implication is vacuously fine there.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**This is exactly Session 3's "not sufficient".** Showing a condition is *not sufficient* meant finding a
case where it holds but the conclusion fails — which is precisely disproving the "for all" that the
sufficiency claim amounts to. Same skill, new name.
:::
:::

## Question 5

::: {.question}
Write the negation of each, as a positive statement.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) For all real $x$, &nbsp; if $x > 2$ then $x^2 > 4$. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) There exists an integer $n$ such that $n$ is prime **and** $n$ is even. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) Every continuous function has a maximum. **[1]**
:::

The quantifier flips as always, but now the *inside* is itself compound — an implication in (a), an
"and" in (b) — so you must negate **that** correctly too. Recall: [the negation of "if $H$ then $C$" is
"$H$ **and** not $C$"]{.hl}, and the negation of "$P$ and $Q$" is "not $P$ **or** not $Q$". These are the
sub-skills the question is really testing.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — negating a statement with a condition inside
:::


**(a)** Flip *for all* → *there exists*, and negate the implication. The negation of "if $x>2$ then
$x^2>4$" is "$x>2$ **and** $x^2 \le 4$":

> **There exists a real $x$ such that $x > 2$ and $x^2 \le 4$.**

*(This happens to be false — the original is true — but the negation is formed correctly all the same.)*

**(b)** Flip *there exists* → *for all*, and negate "prime and even". By De Morgan, "not (prime and even)"
is "not prime **or** not even":

> **For all integers $n$, &nbsp; $n$ is not prime or $n$ is not even** &nbsp;(equivalently: $n$ is not
> prime, or $n$ is odd).

**(c)** "Every continuous function has a maximum" is a *for all*; negate to a *there exists*:

> **There exists a continuous function with no maximum.** *(True — e.g. $f(x)=x$ on all of $\mathbb R$.)*

$\blacksquare$

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| (a) negating "if $x>2$ then $x^2>4$" to "if $x>2$ then $x^2\le4$" | The negation of an implication is **not** another implication. It is "$H$ **and** not $C$". |
| (b) "for all $n$, $n$ is not prime **and** not even" | Negating "and" gives "**or**", by De Morgan — not "and". |
| Forgetting to flip the quantifier at all | Both the quantifier **and** the inside must change. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:8cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — negating what's inside

Once the quantifier is flipped, negate the interior with these standard moves:

| Inside | Its negation |
|---|---|
| $P$ **and** $Q$ | not $P$ **or** not $Q$ &nbsp;*(De Morgan)* |
| $P$ **or** $Q$ | not $P$ **and** not $Q$ &nbsp;*(De Morgan)* |
| **if** $H$ **then** $C$ | $H$ **and** not $C$ |
| $x > a$ | $x \le a$ |

**The implication one is the trap.** *"if $H$ then $C$"* promises you never get $H$-true-with-$C$-false —
so the only way to break it is exactly $H$ **and** not $C$. Its negation is **not** "if $H$ then not $C$".

Put together with the quantifier rule, a full negation is two steps:

$$\text{not}\big(\text{for all } x,\ \text{if } H \text{ then } C\big) = \text{there exists } x \text{ such that } H \text{ and not } C.$$

This exact shape — *"there is an $x$ satisfying the hypothesis but not the conclusion"* — is what a
counterexample to a theorem always looks like.
:::

# Part 3 — Hard

## Question 6

::: {.question}
For real numbers, consider the two statements:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**P:** For all $x$, there exists $y$ such that $y > x$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**Q:** There exists $y$ such that for all $x$, $y > x$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Explain the difference in meaning between **P** and **Q**. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) State, with reasons, whether each is true. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) Write the negation of **P**. **[1]**
:::

The two statements use the **same words in a different order**, and they mean different things — this is
the subtlest point in the whole quantifier topic. [In **P** the $y$ may depend on $x$ (choose it after);
in **Q** a single $y$ must work for every $x$ at once.]{.hl} Read each literally, left to right, and ask
at each step "does this thing get to see the one before it?"

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — statements with two quantifiers, and their order
:::


**(a)** In **P**, *"for all $x$"* comes first, so $y$ is chosen **after** $x$ and may depend on it:
*given any $x$, I can find some larger $y$.* In **Q**, *"there exists $y$"* comes first, so **one** $y$
must be fixed **before** $x$ and then beat **every** $x$: *there is a single number bigger than
everything.*

**(b)**

- **P is true.** Given any real $x$, take $y = x+1$; then $y > x$. The choice of $y$ depends on $x$,
  which **P** allows.
- **Q is false.** It claims a largest real number exists — one $y$ above all $x$. But whatever $y$ you
  fix, $x = y+1$ is larger, so no such $y$ exists.

**(c)** Negate **P** = *for all $x$, there exists $y$, $y>x$*. Flip each quantifier in turn and negate the
inside ($y>x$ becomes $y \le x$):

> **There exists an $x$ such that for all $y$, &nbsp; $y \le x$.**

*(In words: there is a real number that nothing exceeds — a largest real. False, of course, which fits,
since $P$ was true.)*

$\blacksquare$

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Order of quantifiers changes meaning.** *"for all $x$, there exists $y$"* and *"there exists $y$, for
all $x$"* are **not** interchangeable. Swapping ∀ and ∃ can turn a true statement into a false one, as
here. When you meet two quantifiers, read strictly left to right: each one is chosen knowing only the
ones **before** it.
:::

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| Treating **P** and **Q** as the same | Quantifier **order** matters: in P, $y$ depends on $x$; in Q, one $y$ serves all $x$. |
| Negating **P** by flipping only the first quantifier | **Every** quantifier flips, in order, and the inside is negated. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:9cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — negating a chain of quantifiers

To negate a statement with several quantifiers, **flip every one in turn** (left to right) and negate the
innermost sentence:

$$\text{not}\big(\text{for all } x,\ \text{there exists } y,\ P\big) = \text{there exists } x,\ \text{for all } y,\ \text{not } P.$$

The quantifiers reverse type but **keep their order**; only the sentence at the very end gets negated.

**Reading two quantifiers.** The order is the meaning:

- **for all $x$, there exists $y$** … : $y$ is picked *after* $x$, so it **may depend on $x$**.
- **there exists $y$, for all $x$** … : $y$ is picked *first* and fixed, so **one $y$ must work for
  every $x$**.

The second is the stronger claim. Whenever a Paper 2 question puts a ∀ and an ∃ together, the trap is
almost always that swapping their order looks harmless but changes the truth value.
:::

---

## Question 7

::: {.question}
$n$ denotes a positive integer. Consider the statement

$$\textbf{(S):}\quad \text{For all } n, \text{ if } n \text{ is prime then } n \text{ is odd.}$$

Which of the following is/are correct?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; (S) is true.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; The negation of (S) is *"there exists a prime $n$ that is even"*.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; $n=2$ is a counterexample to (S).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** I only &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** II only &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** III only &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** I and II &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** II and III &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** I and III &nbsp;&nbsp;
**G** I, II and III &nbsp;&nbsp; **H** None
:::

Take the three claims one at a time — they are testing three separate skills from this session: judging
the truth of a "for all", negating it correctly, and recognising a valid counterexample. [Watch how II
and III fit together]{.hl}: the counterexample in III should be exactly the witness that makes the
negation in II true. If II is a correct negation and III is a genuine counterexample, then (S) must be
false — so I and "II and III" cannot all three hold.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — quantifiers, negation and counterexamples together *(exam-style)*
:::


Deal with each in turn.

**I — is (S) true?** (S) says every prime is odd. But $2$ is prime and even, so (S) is **false**.
So **I is incorrect.**

**II — is the negation right?** (S) is *for all $n$, if prime then odd*. Its negation flips to *there
exists $n$* and negates the implication ("prime and not odd"):
$$\text{there exists } n \text{ such that } n \text{ is prime and } n \text{ is not odd,}$$
i.e. *there exists a prime that is even.* That is exactly statement II. **II is correct.** ✓

**III — is $n=2$ a counterexample?** A counterexample to (S) must satisfy the hypothesis (prime) and
break the conclusion (odd). $n=2$ is prime and not odd, so it does both. **III is correct.** ✓

So **II and III** are correct and I is not — **option E**. $\blacksquare$

*Consistency check: II gives the negation, III supplies the witness that makes that negation true —
together they confirm (S) is false, which is why I fails. The three answers hang together exactly as they
should.*

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| Marking I correct — "primes are usually odd" | *Usually* is not *for all*. $n=2$ makes (S) false. |
| Rejecting II for "not being a for-all" | The negation of a "for all" **is** a "there exists". That is correct, not a mistake. |
| Marking III wrong because "$2$ is a special case" | A single valid counterexample is a complete disproof — special cases are exactly what you want. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:9cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — the whole session on one question

This question stitches together everything in S4, and the pieces are meant to be checked for consistency:

$$\underbrace{\text{(S) is false}}_{\text{I}} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \underbrace{\text{its negation is true}}_{\text{II}} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \underbrace{\text{a counterexample exists}}_{\text{III}} .$$

These three are logically **the same fact** seen three ways. So a self-consistent answer can never have I
true *and* III true — a counterexample existing is precisely what makes (S) false.

**The exam habit:** when a question asks about a statement's truth, its negation, and a counterexample all
at once, work out the negation first (it tells you what a counterexample must look like), then hunt for
that counterexample, then read the truth of the original off whether you found one.
:::

# Part 4 — Exam bank: mock papers

Five from exam-style mock material, in the order the skill is built: **negate one statement**, then
**judge whether $\forall\exists$ statements are true**, then **work with a definition that is itself a
quantifier chain**. The two rules below are used by everything in Parts 4 and 5 alike.

::: {.callout-important}
## The two rules everything below uses

**Negating flips every quantifier, in order, and then negates the inside.**
$$\lnot\big(\forall x,\ P(x)\big)=\exists x,\ \lnot P(x)\qquad\qquad
\lnot\big(\exists x,\ P(x)\big)=\forall x,\ \lnot P(x)$$

**Order matters, and this is the difference the exam tests.**

- $\forall x\,\exists y$ — *$y$ is allowed to depend on $x$*: pick $x$ first, then find a $y$ to suit it.
- $\exists y\,\forall x$ — *one single $y$ must work for every $x$ at once.* Far stronger.

Swapping the two is the single most common error in this part of the paper.
:::

---

## Question 8 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set C · P2 Q11</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the statement: &nbsp;*$f(x)>g(x)$ for all real values of $x>a$.*

Which one of the following is a **negation** of this statement?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $f(x)\le g(x)$ for at least one real value of $x>a$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $f(x)\le g(x)$ for all real values of $x>a$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $f(x)\le g(x)$ for at least one real value of $x\le a$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $f(x)\le g(x)$ for no real values of $x>a$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $f(x)>g(x)$ for at least one real value of $x\le a$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** $f(x)>g(x)$ for at least one real value of $x>a$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** $f(x)>g(x)$ for all real values of $x\le a$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** $f(x)>g(x)$ for no real values of $x>a$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Easy — the rule applied once)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**A.** The statement is $\;\forall x>a,\ f(x)>g(x)$. Negating does exactly two things:

1. $\forall$ becomes $\exists$: "for all $x>a$" $\to$ "for **at least one** $x>a$";
2. the inside is negated: $f(x)>g(x)$ $\to$ $f(x)\le g(x)$.

Giving *"$f(x)\le g(x)$ for at least one real value of $x>a$"* — option **A**.

**What the distractors change, and why each is wrong:**

- **The range stays $x>a$.** Options **C**, **E** and **G** switch to $x\le a$. *The negation of "for all
  $x$ in a range" never changes the range* — it changes how many of them you need.
- **B** negates the inside but keeps $\forall$: "$f\le g$ **everywhere**" is far stronger than the negation.
  The opposite of "always above" is "not always above", not "always below".
- **D** and **H** say "for no values", which is another $\forall$ in disguise ("for all $x>a$, *not* …").

*If you take one thing from this question:* **"not always" means "at least once", never "never".**
$\;\blacksquare$
:::

## Question 9 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set D · P2 Q18</span>

::: {.question}
Which of the following statements, taken independently, is/are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; **For all** real $x$, **there exists** a real $y$ such that $y^{2}=x$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; **There exists** a real $y$ such that **for all** positive real $x$, $y^{2}=x$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; **For all** real $y$, **there exists** a non-negative real $x$ such that $y^{2}=x$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp;
**E** I and II only &nbsp; **F** II and III only &nbsp; **G** I and III only &nbsp; **H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Medium — one equation, three different questions)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**D — III only.** All three statements use the same equation $y^{2}=x$. *What changes is which letter is
chosen first, and what it is allowed to depend on.*

- **I — false.** "For all real $x$" includes **negative** $x$, and $y^{2}=x$ has no real solution when
  $x<0$. One value, $x=-1$, kills it.
- **II — false.** Here a **single** $y$ must satisfy $y^{2}=x$ for **every** positive $x$ at once — so $y^2$
  would have to equal $1$ and $2$ simultaneously. *This is the $\exists\forall$ trap:* the statement looks
  like I with the words shuffled, but it is enormously stronger.
- **III — true.** Now $y$ is given first and $x$ is chosen afterwards, so simply **take $x=y^{2}$**. It is
  non-negative, as required, for every real $y$. ✓

*Compare I and III carefully — they are near-mirror images.* I asks "is every real number a square?"
(**no**); III asks "does every real number have a square?" (**yes**). The mathematics is trivial; reading
the quantifier order correctly is the whole question. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

## Question 10 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set B · P2 Q19</span>

::: {.question}
Which of the following statements are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; **There exists** a real $y$ such that **for all** real $x$, $y>x$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; **There exists** a real $x$ such that **for all** real $y$, $x+y>xy$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; **For all** real $x$, **there exists** a real $y$ such that $x-y=xy^{2}+1$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp;
**E** I and II only &nbsp; **F** II and III only &nbsp; **G** I and III only &nbsp; **H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Hard — to prove $\exists$, produce the witness)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**F — II and III.**

- **I — false.** It claims there is a **largest real number**: a single $y$ beating every $x$. But $y+1$ is
  real and $y+1>y$, so no such $y$ exists.
- **II — true.** *To prove an $\exists$ statement, you only have to exhibit one value.* Take $x=1$: then
  $x+y=1+y$ and $xy=y$, so the claim becomes $1+y>y$ — true for every real $y$. ✓
- **III — true**, and the same way. Rearrange to $xy^{2}+y+1-x=0$ and look for a $y$ that works for **every**
  $x$. Try $y=-1$:
  $$x(-1)^{2}+(-1)+1-x=x-1+1-x=0\quad\text{✓ for all }x .$$
  So $y=-1$ is a witness for every $x$ at once — III holds.

*(If the witness is not spotted, the discriminant route also works: for $x\neq0$ the quadratic in $y$ has
discriminant $1-4x(1-x)=4x^{2}-4x+1=(2x-1)^{2}\ge0$, so a real $y$ always exists; and $x=0$ gives
$y=-1$ directly.)*

**The exam habit.** $\exists$ statements are **cheap to prove and expensive to disprove** — find one value.
$\forall$ statements are the reverse — find one counterexample. Statement I is a $\exists\forall$, so
disproving it needed an argument, not an example; II and III only needed $x=1$ and $y=-1$.
$\;\blacksquare$
:::

## Question 11 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock C · P2 Q1</span>

::: {.question}
Let $n$ denote a positive integer. Consider the following three statements.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; **For every** $n$, if $n^{2}$ is divisible by $12$, then $n$ is divisible by $6$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; **For every** $n$, if $n^{2}$ is divisible by $12$, then $n$ is divisible by $12$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; **There exists** an $n$ such that $n^{2}$ is divisible by $12$ but $n$ is not
divisible by $12$.

Which of the statements are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** I only &nbsp; **B** II only &nbsp; **C** III only &nbsp; **D** I and II only &nbsp;
**E** II and III only &nbsp; **F** I and III only &nbsp; **G** all of them
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Medium — II and III are exact opposites)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**F — I and III.**

**Notice the structure before doing any arithmetic:** III is precisely the **negation of II**
($\lnot\forall n(H\Rightarrow C)=\exists n(H\text{ and }\lnot C)$). So exactly one of II and III is
true — which immediately rules out options **B**, **C**, **D** and **G** *(they either keep both or drop
both)*.

- **I — true.** $12=2^{2}\times3$, so $12\mid n^{2}$ gives $3\mid n^{2}$ and $4\mid n^{2}$. Since $3$ is
  **prime**, $3\mid n^{2}$ forces $3\mid n$; and $4\mid n^{2}$ forces $n$ to be even, so $2\mid n$. Having
  both factors, $6\mid n$. ✓
- **II — false**, and **III — true**, on the same single example: $n=6$ gives $n^{2}=36=12\times3$, so
  $12\mid n^{2}$, yet $12\nmid6$.

*Why I works but II does not:* squaring **doubles** every exponent, so $n^{2}$ carrying $2^{2}$ only forces
$n$ to carry $2^{1}$. You recover $6=2\times3$, never the second factor of $2$ needed for $12$.

**This is the same fact as [S5 Question 30](s05_proof_methods.qmd)**, where $n=6$ and $n=18$ appear as the
counterexamples to exactly statement II. Here it is dressed as a quantifier question instead.
$\;\blacksquare$
:::

Working
:::

## Question 12 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock E · P2 Q11</span>

::: {.question}
Let $f$ be a real function and let $a$ be a real number. We say that $f$ is **smoothly joined** at $x=a$ if
and only if

> for every real number $h>0$, there exists a real number $d>0$ such that, for every real number $x$, if
> $\lvert x-a\rvert<d$ then $\lvert f(x)-f(a)\rvert<h$.

Which of the following means that $f$ is **not** smoothly joined at $x=a$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** For every $h>0$, for every $d>0$, there exists $x$ such that $\lvert x-a\rvert<d$ and $\lvert f(x)-f(a)\rvert\ge h$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** There exists $h>0$ such that there exists $d>0$ such that, for every $x$, if $\lvert x-a\rvert<d$ then $\lvert f(x)-f(a)\rvert\ge h$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** There exists $h>0$ such that, for every $d>0$, there exists $x$ such that $\lvert x-a\rvert<d$ and $\lvert f(x)-f(a)\rvert\ge h$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** There exists $h>0$ such that, for every $d>0$, for every $x$, if $\lvert x-a\rvert<d$ then $\lvert f(x)-f(a)\rvert\ge h$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** For every $h>0$, there exists $d>0$ such that, for every $x$, if $\lvert x-a\rvert<d$ then $\lvert f(x)-f(a)\rvert\ge h$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Hard — three quantifiers and an implication)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**C.** The definition, stripped to symbols, is
$$\forall h>0\ \ \exists d>0\ \ \forall x\ \ \big(\lvert x-a\rvert<d\Rightarrow\lvert f(x)-f(a)\rvert<h\big).$$

**Negate from the outside in, one layer at a time.** Each quantifier flips, and only at the very end do you
touch the mathematics:

| Layer | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $\forall h>0$ | $\exists h>0$ |
| 2 | $\exists d>0$ | $\forall d>0$ |
| 3 | $\forall x$ | $\exists x$ |
| 4 | $\lvert x-a\rvert<d\Rightarrow\lvert f(x)-f(a)\rvert<h$ | $\lvert x-a\rvert<d$ **and** $\lvert f(x)-f(a)\rvert\ge h$ |

Layer 4 is the step most often dropped: *the negation of "if $P$ then $Q$" is "$P$ **and** $\lnot Q$"* —
**not** "if $P$ then $\lnot Q$". An implication is only false when its hypothesis holds and its conclusion
fails.

Reading the result off: **there exists $h>0$ such that for every $d>0$ there exists $x$ with
$\lvert x-a\rvert<d$ and $\lvert f(x)-f(a)\rvert\ge h$** — option **C**.

**How the wrong options are built:** **A** forgets to flip the first quantifier; **B** flips $\exists d$ the
wrong way *and* keeps the implication; **D** and **E** both keep the implication instead of turning it into
an "and" (**E** additionally leaves the first two quantifiers untouched). *Only C flips all three and
converts the implication.*

*(This is the $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ definition of continuity, with $h$ for $\varepsilon$ and $d$ for
$\delta$. You are not expected to know it — and the question is solvable entirely mechanically, which is the
point.)* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

# Part 5 — Exam bank: real past papers

Quantifiers are the fastest-growing slot on Paper 2. From 2016 to 2020 there was **exactly one** quantifier
question a paper; from 2021 there have been two to four. The seven below are the genuine ones, and they run
in the order the skill is built: judge an ordering, count how often an $\exists$ statement holds, work out
what *"for every $x$"* forces on a polynomial, and finally negate definitions two and three quantifiers
deep.

One habit covers almost all of them. [Before reading a single option, write the statement out as a chain of
symbols]{.hl} — $\forall N\,\exists K\,\forall m$ — because the English hides the order and the symbols
cannot. Then negate in **two separate passes**: flip every quantifier in turn, and only afterwards negate
what is inside. Most wrong options are built by doing one pass and forgetting the other.


## Question 13 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2022 · P2 Q10 &nbsp;◆</span>

::: {.question}
Which of the following statements is/are true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; For **all** real numbers $x$ and for **all** positive integers $n$, $\;x<n$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; For **all** real numbers $x$, **there exists** a positive integer $n$ such that $\;x<n$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; **There exists** a real number $x$ such that for **all** positive integers $n$, $\;x<n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp;
**E** I and II only &nbsp; **F** I and III only &nbsp; **G** II and III only &nbsp; **H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Hard — a real TMUA question; three orderings of one inequality)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**G — II and III.** The inequality $x<n$ never changes; only **who is chosen first** does.

- **I — false.** It claims every real is below every positive integer simultaneously. $x=100$, $n=1$ ends it.
- **II — true.** For each real $x$ you choose $n$ **afterwards**, so $n$ may depend on $x$: take
  $n=\lfloor x\rfloor+1$ (or $n=1$ when $x<1$). There is always a positive integer above any given real.
- **III — true.** Now you need **one** real that beats every positive integer at once — and $x=0$ does it,
  since $0<n$ for every positive integer $n$. *(Any $x\le0$ works.)*

**The pairing to notice.** II and III are $\forall\exists$ and $\exists\forall$ of the same inequality, and
here **both** happen to be true — which is why this question is harder than the usual "one of them fails".
$\exists\forall$ is normally the stronger claim, but the inequality points the convenient way: it asks the
real number to be **small**, and $0$ is small enough for all $n$ at once.

*The common slip is doubting **II**.* "$\forall x\,\exists n$" allows a **different $n$ for each $x$** —
that is exactly the Archimedean property of the reals, and it is what separates II from the blanket claim
in I. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 14 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2023 · P2 Q19 &nbsp;◆</span>

::: {.question}
$f$ is a non-constant polynomial and $g(x)=x\,f''(x)$. Suppose $f(x)=0$ for exactly $M$ real values of $x$,
and $g(x)=0$ for exactly $N$ real values of $x$. Which of the following are **possible**?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $M<N$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **II** &nbsp; $M=N$ &nbsp;&nbsp; **III** &nbsp; $M>N$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp;
**E** I and II only &nbsp; **F** I and III only &nbsp; **G** II and III only &nbsp; **H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

[*(Hard — a real TMUA question; "possible" is an $\exists$)*]{style="color:#7a5195"}
**H — all three.**

**Read the word "possible" as a quantifier.** "$M<N$ is possible" means *"**there exists** a polynomial $f$
with $M<N$"* — so each statement is an $\exists$, and **an $\exists$ is proved by producing one example**.
Three statements, three examples; no general theory is needed.

*First note what $g=0$ means:* $g(x)=x\,f''(x)$ vanishes when $x=0$ **or** $f''(x)=0$. So $N$ counts the root
$x=0$ together with the real roots of $f''$ — and $x=0$ is always available, which is what makes $N$ easy to
control.

| | want | take $f$ | $M$ | $g=xf''$ | $N$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **I** | $M<N$ | $x^{4}+1$ | $0$ — *never zero* | $12x^{3}$ | $1$ &nbsp;($x=0$) |
| **II** | $M=N$ | $x^{2}$ | $1$ &nbsp;($x=0$) | $2x$ | $1$ &nbsp;($x=0$) |
| **III** | $M>N$ | $x^{4}-5x^{2}+4$ | $4$ &nbsp;($\pm1,\pm2$) | $x\left(12x^{2}-10\right)$ | $3$ &nbsp;($0,\pm\sqrt{5/6}$) |

All three orderings occur, so **H**.

**Why this is easier than it looks.** The instinct is to hunt for a relationship between the roots of $f$ and
the roots of $f''$ — but there is none to find, and the question never asks for one. *It asks only whether
each ordering can happen at all*, and one witness settles each. Compare **Question 10**: proving $\exists$
cost one value of $x$ there, and one polynomial here.

*The mirror-image trap:* had the question asked which ordering **must** hold, a single example would prove
nothing and you would need an argument covering every $f$. **"Possible" and "always" demand opposite kinds of
work** — read which one you were given before starting. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:5cm"}

:::

## Question 15 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2022 · P2 Q13</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the statement $(*)$ about a real number $x$:

> $(*)$ &nbsp; **There exists** a real number $y$ such that $\;x-xy+y\;$ is negative.

For how many real values of $x$ is $(*)$ true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** no values of $x$ &nbsp; **B** exactly one value of $x$ &nbsp; **C** exactly two values of $x$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** all except exactly two values of $x$ &nbsp; **E** all except exactly one value of $x$ &nbsp;
**F** all values of $x$
:::

The quantifier tells you which letter is yours. *"There exists a real number $y$"* means $y$ is the free
choice and $x$ is a constant — so [collect the expression in powers of $y$, not $x$]{.hl}, and ask what
values it can be made to reach.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — an $\exists$ statement over a linear expression; when can it fail?
:::

**E — all except exactly one value of $x$.**

**Collect in $y$.**

$$x-xy+y \;=\; x + y(1-x)$$

As a function of $y$ this is a straight line with gradient $1-x$ and intercept $x$.

**Case $x\neq1$.** The gradient $1-x$ is non-zero, so as $y$ runs over the reals the expression runs over
**every** real value — negative ones included. So $(*)$ is true. Explicitly:

| | need | a $y$ that works |
|---|---|---|
| $x<1$ &nbsp;(gradient positive) | $x+y(1-x)<0$ | any $y<\dfrac{-x}{1-x}$ |
| $x>1$ &nbsp;(gradient negative) | $x+y(1-x)<0$ | any $y>\dfrac{-x}{1-x}$ |

*Check:* $x=0$ needs $y<0$; $x=2$ gives $2-y$, negative once $y>2$; $x=-3$ gives $-3+4y$, negative once
$y<\tfrac34$. ✓

**Case $x=1$.** The $y$-term dies:

$$x-xy+y \;=\; 1-y+y \;=\; 1 ,$$

which is $1$ for **every** $y$ — never negative. So $(*)$ is false, and $x=1$ is the only exception.

Exactly one value of $x$ fails, so the answer is **E**.

**The lesson.** *An $\exists$ statement about a linear expression is almost always true* — a line with
non-zero gradient reaches everything. [The only way it can fail is if the variable you are allowed to
choose disappears from the expression]{.hl}, so the whole question is: for which $x$ does the coefficient
of $y$ vanish? $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 16 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2021 · P2 Q13</span>

::: {.question}
A region $R$ in the $(x,y)$-plane is defined by the simultaneous inequalities

$$y-x<3 \qquad\qquad y-x^{2}<1$$

Which of the following statements is/are true for **every** point in $R$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $-1<x<2$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $(y-x)\left(y-x^{2}\right)<3$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; $y<5$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp;
**E** I and II only &nbsp; **F** I and III only &nbsp; **G** II and III only &nbsp; **H** I, II and III
:::

Both inequalities say *less than*, so $R$ is what lies **below both** curves. That is the whole question:
the two boundaries cross at $x=-1$ and $x=2$, and [those crossing points would bound $R$ only if $R$ were
the region *between* the curves]{.hl}. Sketch it before judging anything.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — a "for every point" claim, and how an unbounded region defeats it
:::

**A — none of them.**

```{python}
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 5.0))
x = np.linspace(-6, 12, 1200)
line, para = x + 3, x**2 + 1

ax.plot(x, line, color='#2ca02c', lw=2.2, label='$y=x+3$')
ax.plot(x, para, color='#1f77b4', lw=2.2, label='$y=x^{2}+1$')
ax.fill_between(x, np.minimum(line, para), -60, color='#7a5195', alpha=0.16,
                label='$R$ — below BOTH curves')

notes = [(10, 12, '$(10,\\,12)\\in R$: kills I ($x>2$)\nand III ($y>5$)', -206, -46),
         (1, -9, '$(1,\\,-9)\\in R$, and here\n$(y-x)(y-x^{2})=100$: kills II', 34, -40)]
for xv, yv, txt, dx, dy in notes:
    ax.plot([xv], [yv], 'o', color='#d62728', ms=8, zorder=5)
    ax.annotate(txt, (xv, yv), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(dx, dy), fontsize=9,
                color='#d62728', arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='#d62728', lw=1.2))

ax.axhline(5, color='0.5', lw=1.0, ls=':')
ax.text(-5.7, 6.4, '$y=5$', fontsize=9, color='0.4')
ax.axvline(-1, color='0.5', lw=1.0, ls=':'); ax.axvline(2, color='0.5', lw=1.0, ls=':')
ax.text(-5.7, -52, 'the curves cross at $x=-1$ and $x=2$,\nbut they do not enclose $R$',
        fontsize=9, color='0.35')

ax.set_xlim(-6, 12); ax.set_ylim(-60, 40)
ax.set_xlabel('$x$'); ax.set_ylabel('$y$')
ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc='upper left', framealpha=0.95)
ax.spines['top'].set_visible(False); ax.spines['right'].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

$R$ is everything underneath the lower of the two curves. *It runs to every value of $x$ and downwards
without limit* — so any claim that bounds $x$ or $y$ from one side is in trouble.

### I is false

Take $(10,12)$. Then $y-x=2<3$ ✓ and $y-x^{2}=12-100=-88<1$ ✓, so the point is in $R$ — and $x=10$ is
nowhere near $-1<x<2$. *The values $-1$ and $2$ are where $x+3=x^{2}+1$; they would bound the region lying
between the curves, and $R$ is not that region.*

### III is false

The same point: $y=12>5$. *Once $x$ is free to be large, $y$ can sit just under the line $y=x+3$ and be as
large as you like.*

### II is false

Take $(1,-9)$: $y-x=-10<3$ ✓ and $y-x^{2}=-9-1=-10<1$ ✓, so it is in $R$, and

$$(y-x)\left(y-x^{2}\right)=(-10)\times(-10)=100 ,$$

which is not less than $3$. *Both bracketed quantities are negative deep inside $R$, and multiplying two
large negatives gives a large positive — so the product has no upper bound at all.* Multiplying two
inequalities of the form "$<$" is only safe when both sides are positive.

Since all three fail, the answer is **A**.

**The lesson.** [A "true for every point in $R$" claim dies the moment $R$ is unbounded in a direction the
claim forgot about]{.hl}. Before testing anything, ask how far $R$ extends — and test a point far out, not
a comfortable one near the origin. *Here a single far-out point disposed of two statements at once.*
$\;\blacksquare$
:::

## Question 17 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2020 · P2 Q18</span>

::: {.question}
In this question, $\mathrm{f}(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d$ and $\mathrm{g}(x)=px^{3}+qx^{2}+rx+s$ are cubic
polynomials.

If $\;\mathrm{f}(x)-\mathrm{g}(x)>0\;$ for **every** real $x$, which of the following is/are
**necessarily** true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; $a>p$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; if $b=q$ then $c=r$
&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; $d>s$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp;
**E** I and II only &nbsp; **F** I and III only &nbsp; **G** II and III only &nbsp; **H** I, II and III
:::

Write $\mathrm{h}(x)=\mathrm{f}(x)-\mathrm{g}(x)$. It is a difference of two cubics, so it is a cubic **or
less** — and that *"or less"* is the whole question. [A "for every real $x$" condition is a statement about
what happens as $\lvert x\rvert$ grows]{.hl} as much as about any particular value, so look at the leading
term first.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — what "for every real $x$" forces on a polynomial; an equality disguised as an inequality
:::

**G — II and III only.**

Write

$$\mathrm{h}(x)=\underbrace{(a-p)}_{A}x^{3}+\underbrace{(b-q)}_{B}x^{2}+\underbrace{(c-r)}_{C}x+\underbrace{(d-s)}_{D}
\;>\;0\quad\text{for every real }x .$$

### Step 1 — the cubic term must disappear

Suppose $A\neq0$. Then $\mathrm{h}$ is a genuine cubic, and a cubic takes **every** real value: as
$x\to-\infty$ it runs to $-\infty$ (if $A>0$) or as $x\to+\infty$ it does (if $A<0$). Either way
$\mathrm{h}$ is negative somewhere, contradicting the hypothesis.

*Concretely, even $x^{3}+1000$ — huge constant, tiny-looking cubic — is $-999000$ at $x=-100$.* No cubic
term survives a "positive for every $x$" condition.

$$\boxed{A=0,\ \text{that is } a=p}$$

### Step 2 — read off the three statements

**I is false — and not merely unproved.** Step 1 shows $a=p$ is **forced**, so $a>p$ is impossible.
*This is the trap: the question offers an inequality where the truth is an equality, and "$a>p$" looks
like the natural thing to deduce from "$\mathrm{f}>\mathrm{g}$".*

**III is true, in one line.** Put $x=0$:

$$\mathrm{h}(0)=D=d-s>0 .$$

*Every "for every $x$" hypothesis can be used at any single $x$ you like, and $x=0$ is the cheapest.*

**II is true.** With $A=0$, $\mathrm{h}(x)=Bx^{2}+Cx+D$. Now suppose $b=q$, i.e. $B=0$. Then
$\mathrm{h}(x)=Cx+D$. A linear function with $C\neq0$ is negative for large $\lvert x\rvert$ — for instance
$x+1000$ is negative at $x=-2000$ — so we must have $C=0$, i.e. $\;c=r$. ✓

So **II and III only: G**.

**The lesson.** Two moves handle every question of this shape. [Kill the top-degree term by looking at
infinity, then evaluate at $x=0$]{.hl}. The first tells you which coefficients are *equal*; the second
hands you the constant term for free. *Note how differently the three statements behave: one is impossible,
one is one line, and one needs the argument repeated a degree lower.* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

## Question 18 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2017 · P2 Q17</span>

::: {.question}
A set $S$ of whole numbers is called **stapled** if and only if for every whole number $a$ which is in $S$
there exists a prime factor of $a$ which divides at least one other number in $S$.

Let $T$ be a set of whole numbers. Which of the following is true **if and only if** $T$ is **not**
stapled?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** &nbsp; For every number $a$ in $T$, there is **no** prime factor of $a$ which divides **every** other number in $T$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** &nbsp; For every number $a$ in $T$, there is **no** prime factor of $a$ which divides **at least one** other number in $T$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** &nbsp; For every number $a$ in $T$, there **is** a prime factor of $a$ which does **not** divide **any** other number in $T$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** &nbsp; For every number $a$ in $T$, there **is** a prime factor of $a$ which does **not** divide **at least one** other number in $T$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** &nbsp; There **exists** a number $a$ in $T$ such that there is **no** prime factor of $a$ which divides **every** other number in $T$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** &nbsp; There **exists** a number $a$ in $T$ such that there is **no** prime factor of $a$ which divides **at least one** other number in $T$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** &nbsp; There **exists** a number $a$ in $T$ such that there **is** a prime factor of $a$ which does **not** divide **any** other number in $T$.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** &nbsp; There **exists** a number $a$ in $T$ such that there **is** a prime factor of $a$ which does **not** divide **at least one** other number in $T$.
:::

Do not read the options first — they are designed to be read first. [Write the definition as a chain of
quantifiers, negate it mechanically, and only then go looking for your own sentence in the list]{.hl}. The
eight options are precisely the eight ways of getting one step of that wrong.

Note also that **no arithmetic is required**: "prime factor" could be replaced by any relation at all and
the answer would not change.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — negating a two-quantifier definition; $\lnot\exists p$ is "no $p$", never "some $p$ fails"
:::

**F.**

### Step 1 — write the definition in symbols

Let $D(a,p)$ mean *"$p$ divides at least one other number in the set"*. Then

$$S \text{ is stapled} \iff \forall a\in S,\ \exists p \text{ a prime factor of } a,\ D(a,p).$$

### Step 2 — negate, one quantifier at a time

$$\lnot\big(\forall a\ \exists p\ D\big)\;=\;\exists a\ \lnot\big(\exists p\ D\big)\;=\;\exists a\ \forall p\ \lnot D .$$

In English: **there is a number $a$ in $T$ for which *no* prime factor of $a$ divides at least one other
number in $T$.** That is exactly **F**.

### Step 3 — why each of the others fails

| options | what went wrong |
|---|---|
| **A, B, C, D** | all begin *"For every number $a$"* — the outer $\forall$ was never flipped. *Four options gone on the first move, before the inner clause is even read.* |
| **E** | correct outer $\exists$, correct *"there is no prime factor"*, but the inner predicate was changed from *divides **at least one** other* to *divides **every** other*. A different statement about a different property. |
| **G** | says *"there **is** a prime factor which does not divide any other"* — that is $\exists p\,\lnot D$, not $\lnot\exists p\,D$. *It claims **one** prime factor fails; the negation needs **all** of them to fail.* |
| **H** | the same $\exists p$ error as G, and the inner clause mangled on top. |

### The lesson

Two of those rows are the same mistake in different places, and it is the one worth memorising:

$$\lnot\big(\exists p,\ D(p)\big)\;=\;\forall p,\ \lnot D(p)\qquad\text{— "no } p \text{ works"},$$

[**not** "there is a $p$ that fails"]{.hl}. In English the two sound almost identical, which is why the
exam can build four wrong options out of the difference. *Symbols do not have this ambiguity; that is the
entire reason for translating first.* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

## Question 19 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2018 · P2 Q12</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following statement:

> For any positive integer $N$ there is a positive integer $K$ such that $N(Km+1)-1$ is **not prime for
> any** positive integer $m$.

Which one of the following is the **negation** of this statement?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** &nbsp; For any positive integer $N$ there is a positive integer $K$ such that there is a positive integer $m$ for which $N(Km+1)-1$ is prime.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** &nbsp; For any positive integer $N$ there is a positive integer $K$ such that there is a positive integer $m$ for which $N(Km+1)-1$ is not prime.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** &nbsp; For any positive integer $N$ there is a positive integer $K$ such that for any positive integer $m$, $N(Km+1)-1$ is not prime.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** &nbsp; For any positive integer $N$, any positive integer $K$ and any positive integer $m$, $N(Km+1)-1$ is not prime.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** &nbsp; There is a positive integer $N$ such that for any positive integer $K$ there is a positive integer $m$ for which $N(Km+1)-1$ is not prime.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** &nbsp; There is a positive integer $N$ such that for any positive integer $K$ there is a positive integer $m$ for which $N(Km+1)-1$ is prime.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** &nbsp; There is a positive integer $N$ such that for any positive integer $K$ and any positive integer $m$, $N(Km+1)-1$ is prime.
&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** &nbsp; There is a positive integer $N$ and a positive integer $K$ for which there is no positive integer $m$ for which $N(Km+1)-1$ is prime.
:::

One phrase decides this question, and it is not a mathematical one: ***"is not prime for any positive
integer $m$"***. In mathematical English, [*"not $P$ for any $m$"* means *"for every $m$, not $P$"*]{.hl} —
it is a $\forall$, not an $\exists$. Misread that and all eight options look reasonable.

Again, no arithmetic is needed. You never have to decide whether the original statement is true.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — negating a three-quantifier chain; the hardest negation in the archive
:::

**F.**

### Step 1 — translate, watching the English

Reading *"not prime for any $m$"* as *"for every $m$, not prime"*:

$$\text{original}\;=\;\forall N\ \exists K\ \forall m\ \big[\,N(Km+1)-1 \text{ is \textbf{not} prime}\,\big]$$

### Step 2 — negate in two passes

**Pass 1 — flip every quantifier, in order.** &nbsp; $\forall N\,\exists K\,\forall m\;\longrightarrow\;\exists N\,\forall K\,\exists m$

**Pass 2 — negate the inside.** &nbsp; "is not prime" $\longrightarrow$ "**is** prime"

$$\text{negation}\;=\;\exists N\ \forall K\ \exists m\ \big[\,N(Km+1)-1 \text{ is prime}\,\big]$$

In English: *there is a positive integer $N$ such that for any positive integer $K$ there is a positive
integer $m$ for which $N(Km+1)-1$ is prime.* That is **F**.

### Step 3 — the seven wrong options, and which pass each one skipped

| | chain | inside | what is missing |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | $\forall N\ \exists K\ \exists m$ | prime | only the **last** quantifier was flipped |
| **B** | $\forall N\ \exists K\ \exists m$ | not prime | last quantifier flipped, inside not negated |
| **C** | $\forall N\ \exists K\ \forall m$ | not prime | nothing flipped — this **is** the original |
| **D** | $\forall N\ \forall K\ \forall m$ | not prime | a *stronger* claim, not a negation |
| **E** | $\exists N\ \forall K\ \exists m$ | **not** prime | chain perfect, **pass 2 forgotten** |
| **G** | $\exists N\ \forall K\ \forall m$ | prime | third quantifier not flipped |
| **H** | $\exists N\ \exists K\ \forall m$ | not prime | second quantifier not flipped |

**E is the one that catches people.** Its quantifier chain is exactly right, and every instinct says "that
looks like the answer" — but the inner statement was never negated. *A negation is two independent jobs,
and doing one of them perfectly earns nothing.*

**The lesson.** Do the two passes **separately and in writing**. [Flip the quantifiers left to right, then
go back and negate the predicate]{.hl} — never both at once in your head. Six of the seven wrong options
here are built from doing exactly one of those two passes, which tells you how the examiner expects the
mistake to be made. $\;\blacksquare$
:::

:::

**The whole session in one line:**

> **To negate, flip the quantifier and negate the inside. "Not all are Y" means "at least one is not Y" —
> never "none are Y".**

**Next session (S5): proof methods** — direct proof, proof by cases, and proof by contradiction. You have
already met the fourth, disproof by counterexample: it is exactly what you do to a false "for all", which
is why quantifiers came first.

:::
